parts.note: the comedian Dawn French tells a joke, or crack, so a joke from her is a crack belonging to Dawn, which is also the very early hour of daybreak

explanation.surface: Someone asks when it is the right moment to tell a joke in French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' looks like the language, but it is Dawn French, the British comic actress; her crack is her wisecrack.
explanation.definitionFit: Crack of dawn is an idiom for the first light of morning, a time of day.

clue.text: One who figures in the racing world

definitions.text: One who figures in the racing world

parts.words: One who figures in the racing world
parts.note: one who does figures, sums and odds, for the horse-racing business, the turf being the racecourse

explanation.surface: Someone who is a well-known figure at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures in' suggests a prominent person; here it means doing the figures, as a bookmaker works out odds. In Britain a turf accountant is a polite name for a bookie.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker is formally styled this way in Britain, calculating odds and payouts on horse races.

clue.text: In a frenzy, mescalin produces proteins

indicators.note: In tells us the answer is sitting inside the words frenzy and mescalin, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A drug-fuelled frenzy is said to produce certain proteins in the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Enzymes are biological catalysts, and almost all of them are proteins.

parts.note: the novelist Anthony Hope invented a Central European kingdom as the setting for The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.surface: It reads like the patriotic song title Land of Hope and Glory, cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' looks like the abstract virtue, as in the British anthem Land of Hope and Glory; it is the author Anthony Hope.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda is the realm created by author Anthony Hope.

explanation.surface: A foolish lad has taken up heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: Childish behaviour is immature, which makes it silly in the adjectival sense.

clue.text: Supplier of lubricants dealing in coal

indicators.note: dealing, as cards are dealt out, distributes the letters of in coal into a new order

explanation.surface: A fuel merchant who trades in coal also supplies oils.
explanation.definitionFit: An oilcan is the container used to dispense lubricating oil onto machinery.

indicators.note: made from tells us the answer is fashioned out of the letters of hated, worked into another order

explanation.surface: Someone's curtains have been sewn from a fabric they loathe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curtains' looks like drapes; it is the slang for the end of everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Curtains is slang for the end, especially the end of life.

clue.text: Trees with their roots in Jove's acorns!

definitions.text: Trees with their roots in Jove's acorns!

parts.words: Trees with their roots in Jove's acorns!
parts.note: the Latin botanical name juglans comes from Jovis glans, the acorn or nut of Jupiter, so the word's origins lie there

explanation.surface: Trees growing up from acorns dropped by the god Jupiter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roots' means the word's origin rather than the trees' underground parts: the Latin genus name juglans is from Jovis glans, Jove's nut.
explanation.definitionFit: These nut trees belong to the genus Juglans, a name meaning the nut of Jove.

clue.text: With training, she made Sisters leading teachers

indicators.note: training shapes and reforms something, so the letters of she made Sisters are rearranged

explanation.surface: After instruction, a woman turned the nuns into senior educators.
explanation.definitionFit: Headmistresses are the women in charge of schools, the leading teachers there.

clue.text: A flier's device for cutting costs

definitions.note: the definition carries the possessive: a flying bird's

parts.note: a razor is a cutting tool for shaving
a bill is a statement of costs

explanation.surface: An airman's gadget for trimming expenses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot; it is a bird, and the 's is part of the definition, so read 'a bird is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The razorbill is a black and white seabird of the auk family, so it is a flier.

indicators.note: almost means the word stops just short, losing its last letter

parts.note: lee means the sheltered side, away from the wind

explanation.surface: A path that is very nearly entirely protected from the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last L from ALL to leave AL.
explanation.definitionFit: An allee is a formal tree-lined avenue or path in a garden, a place to walk.

clue.text: It's designed to protect from harm etc

indicators.note: from tells us the answer is taken out of the run of letters in harm etc

explanation.surface: A device is designed to keep people safe from harm and the like.
explanation.definitionFit: An armet is a closed medieval helmet, made to protect the wearer's head.

parts.note: a drag is a bore, so a hound that finds hunting a drag; in fact the dog follows a trail of scent dragged across country

explanation.surface: A hound that finds the chase tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: A drag hunt follows an artificial scent laid by dragging a lure; 'a drag' is also slang for something boring.
explanation.definitionFit: This hound is trained to follow an artificial scent trail in place of a live quarry.

explanation.surface: Social functions held on a Sunday have a homely feel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Functions' looks like social events; it is the mathematical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosiness is a warm, comfortable domestic quality, a synonym of homeliness.

clue.text: Stuff the Swiss rolled out for breakfast?

definitions.text: Stuff the Swiss rolled out for breakfast?

parts.words: Stuff the Swiss rolled out for breakfast?
parts.note: rolled oats with fruit and nuts, a cereal mixture introduced from Switzerland

explanation.surface: Something the people of Switzerland serve at the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolled' hints at rolled oats, the cereal's main ingredient, and at a Swiss roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a Swiss breakfast cereal of rolled oats, dried fruit and nuts.

clue.text: Rash result of grasping the nettle?

definitions.text: Rash result of grasping the nettle?

parts.words: Rash result of grasping the nettle?
parts.note: grasping the nettle means facing a problem boldly, but taken literally it gives a stinging skin eruption; the Latin for nettle is urtica

explanation.surface: A hasty consequence of tackling a difficulty head-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like an adjective meaning reckless; it is the noun, a skin eruption.
explanation.definitionFit: Urticaria is the medical name for hives, an itchy rash named after the stinging nettle.

parts.note: Yorick was the jester in Hamlet, and a jester wore a belled cap; a paper size is named after that watermark

explanation.surface: Some paper used to wrap the skull Hamlet holds.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorick is the dead court jester whose skull Hamlet holds; a fool's cap covers a jester's head, and the paper size took its name from a fool's-cap watermark.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolscap is a traditional large size of writing paper.

parts.note: Adam was naked in Eden; dis-covered read as not covered gives a word meaning not clothed

explanation.surface: The circumstances in which the first man was first found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' looks like found; read it as dis-covered, without covering.
explanation.definitionFit: Unclad means naked, which is how Adam appeared before the Fall.

definitions.meaning: the ... pink is a wild dianthus flower found on the cliffs of ... Gorge
a hard English cheese from Somerset

explanation.surface: A cheese with a pinkish colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheddar names both a hard Somerset cheese and a species of wild pink flower.

definitions.meaning: to narrow is to shrink or shorten
a form of the card game bridge in which only tricks bid count towards game

explanation.surface: A bridge that is narrow in span.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to narrow, and contract bridge is the standard form of the card game.

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
mid- tells us to take only the central letters of Wales, without its first and last

parts.note: to post a letter is to put it in the mail

explanation.surface: A missionary has been stationed in central Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' looks like 'placed' in the surface, the missionary being posted; as a piece it is the verb to post, as in mailing a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is one sent out to preach, a missionary such as the early followers of Christ.

definitions.meaning: a viola is a stringed instrument of the violin family, a member of that bowed family

explanation.surface: A drama concerning a character called Viola, as in Twelfth Night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viola' looks like Shakespeare's heroine in Twelfth Night; it is the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiddle means to tinker idly and is also the everyday word for a violin-family instrument.

parts.note: it sounds like commuting on foot, but it is a machine on which people walk to exercise, or once to drive a mill

explanation.surface: Somewhere people go on foot to get to their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk to work' suggests commuting; on this device walking is itself the work, and the word also means monotonous drudgery.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is a moving belt or wheel on which people walk, historically to power machinery.

clue.text: King had one castle in Spain

definitions.meaning: a castle in Spain is an idiom for an impossible daydream or fantasy

explanation.surface: A monarch owned a castle in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' looks like a monarch; it is Martin Luther King and his famous speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream is an aspiration, as in King's speech, and a fanciful daydream like a castle in the air.

definitions.meaning: tight, as in a ... fit or a ... contest, means near and snug

explanation.surface: Something firmly closed.
explanation.definitionFit: Close as a verb means to shut, and as an adjective means tight or near.

indicators.note: out means the remaining letters are put out of order and rearranged
most of means the word loses its end, here its last two letters

explanation.surface: Excavate most of a dungeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims DUNGEON to DUNGE, and 'out' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dig in the ribs is a poke, so dig means a prod with the elbow.

indicators.note: unveiled suggests the words a secret do are opened up and laid out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Newspapers revealed a clandestine party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' looks like newspapers; it is the verb, to hang wallpaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To paper a room is to cover its walls with wallpaper, which decorates it.

parts.note: people who sound off brag; those who blow their own horn literally, brass players, sound all the time

explanation.surface: Players who are forever complaining or showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound off' means to boast or to blow; brass players literally blow their own instrument, the idiom for self-praise.
explanation.definitionFit: These brass musicians perform on a valved horn with a bright, loud tone.
